body_en:
Two arguments are going viral online lately. One says: take all the money spent on aid to Africa — billions of dollars in investment — and hand it to ordinary people instead; everyone would get a decent share. The other says: Trump gave Americans $2,000, so why can't we?

Both sound perfectly reasonable. But each hides several logical fallacies. Let's take them apart, one by one.

1. Handing Out Money Causes Inflation?

The claim:

Inflation is simple: when the amount of goods stays the same but the money in circulation increases, prices go up. Say there are 10 loaves of bread and 100 yuan — each loaf costs 10 yuan. If the money becomes 1,000 yuan but there are still only 10 loaves, each loaf costs 100 yuan. So if we converted all the dollars earned from our trade surplus into yuan and handed them out, prices would definitely soar and money would lose its value.

The rebuttal:

There are errors here in both economics and logic. Economics first, with a simple example:

Suppose you have a cow and the other person has a sheep, and you want to trade. Bartering feels clumsy, so you use a piece of paper marked 10 yuan. That paper can buy either the cow or the sheep. The paper is called money. It only makes exchange easier; it doesn't matter in itself. What matters is the labor behind the cow and the sheep — that's what productivity means.

In other words, you used 10 units of productivity to raise a cow and traded it for a sheep someone else raised with 10 units of productivity. When do the cow and sheep get more expensive? When your village prints too much money. Say there used to be only 10 yuan in circulation, and now the village chief prints 100. Naturally the cow and sheep rise to 100 yuan. That's inflation caused by over-printing money. And the productivity embodied in your cow and sheep hasn't grown at all — it's still 10.

Now suppose you cut your cow in half — 5 units of productivity — exchange it for 5 yuan, and give it to Zhang San. Then you regret it, take the 5 yuan back halfway, and exchange it for half a cow. Will your cow's price go up? Of course not, because no extra money has been printed.

The money spent on aid to Africa represents productivity created by our workers, delivery riders, white-collar workers, scientists, and technicians — the whole of society. That productivity was given away for free. If we take it back halfway, will prices rise? Obviously not, because no money has been printed. If aid money is simply redirected back home, the money supply doesn't change, so there can be no inflation.

So the logical error here is swapping the reallocation of productivity for the printing of money.

In one sentence: if the money being handed out is backed by productivity, it won't cause inflation; if it's printed out of thin air with no productivity behind it, it will. Of course, this sets aside complications like productivity growth and structural mismatch, for the sake of clarity.

2. America Can Hand Out Money Because It Fleeces the World?

The claim:

America can hand out money for a simple reason: the dollar is backed by goods from all over the world. There are so many goods, the pool is so big, that adding a little water barely makes a ripple. So the money they hand out has almost no effect at home — because they're fleecing the whole world.

The rebuttal:

The first half is right; the second half is wrong. The dollar being backed by the world's goods, the pool being big — that's fine. But concluding from that “they fleece the whole world” is a conspiracy theory, and at its core a compound of several fallacies: appeal to ignorance, assuming a conspiracy, unfalsifiability, and false attribution.

What many countries call “handing out money” isn't actually handing out money — it's a tax refund. In other words, it's tax that ordinary people already paid. In hard times, the government shrinks its own spending and returns some of that tax to the people to stimulate the economy. And behind that tax is still productivity: the government's share of productivity shrinks, the people's share grows, and the economy naturally prospers. What does any of that have to do with relations between nations?

Tax refunds come in many more forms, too — tax credits, subsidies, and so on. Blaming a stimulus tool used by many modern countries on fleecing other nations doesn't hold up. If tax refunds were based on fleecing other countries, who is Malaysia fleecing? Who is Singapore fleecing?

3. People Who Demand Handouts Have Ulterior Motives?

The claim:

Why are so many people online today pushing the line that we shouldn't aid Africa or invest in Africa, that we should hand out the money at home? In reality, it's just a bunch of people with ulterior motives misleading ordinary folks.

The rebuttal:

The fallacy here is called appeal to motive. The economics errors have already been taken apart above; here, ordinary people's normal expression of views on public affairs is twisted into “ulterior motives.” The essence is this: instead of discussing whether your argument is sound, it questions you as a person.

4. Endure Together, and Once the Yuan Becomes the World Currency, All Will Be Well?

The claim:

We really must not let others stir us up. We must think for ourselves about why the country does this, and unite to get through this hardest period together. In the future, when our renminbi becomes the world's common currency, we and our children and grandchildren will all be very happy. Imagine the America of the 1960s and 70s, when a blue-collar worker could support a family of five. Once we become number one in the world, we will have days like that too. Let's unite and push forward together.

The rebuttal:

The fallacies here are emotional blackmail and false analogy.

The message is: you have to endure hardship together, and if you complain instead of enduring, you've been stirred up. It's a classic emotional blackmail script — turning a discussion of public issues into being stirred up, turning a discussion of gains and losses into undermining unity, turning a question of logic into a question of attitude.

The other fallacy is false analogy. Americans were able to live well not because the dollar became the world currency. The reasons are far more complicated: World War II barely touched the American homeland, so there was almost no cost of postwar reconstruction; unions were extremely strong; a model of high taxes plus rational fiscal allocation; the golden age of manufacturing, and more. Using America as an analogy to prove the power of a world currency is plainly absurd.

Conclusion

The problem with these arguments isn't just logic. They also exploit the public's lack of basic economics knowledge, coaxing people to endure hardship quietly instead of asking for their share of the pie.

But for us ordinary people, a little knowledge of logic and economics is enough to see through their lies at a glance.
excerpt_en: Hand the billions spent on aid to Africa back to ordinary people — would prices explode? No. The money already exists; moving it isn't printing it. Four popular arguments, four logical fallacies, taken apart one by one.
title_en: Logic Check: Would Giving Africa Aid Money to Ordinary People Really Cause Inflation?
